title: Milgram (1963) Obedience Study
summary: Extraction of all examinable knowledge points from the Milgram (1963) obedience study notes.

knowledge.text: Aim: to investigate how far people would obey an authority figure instructing them to harm another person.
Sample: 40 American men aged 20-50 from New Haven, recruited by newspaper advert, paid $4.50 (volunteer / self-selected sample).
Procedure: lab at Yale University. Participant always assigned role of teacher; a confederate (Mr Wallace) was the learner.
Procedure: Teacher gave electric shocks (fake) from 15V to 450V in 15V steps for wrong answers on a word-pair task.
Procedure: Experimenter in grey lab coat used four verbal prods.
Verbal prod 1: Please continue
Verbal prod 2: The experiment requires that you continue
Verbal prod 3: It is absolutely essential that you continue
Verbal prod 4: You have no other choice, you must go on
Procedure: Learner pounded on wall at 300V and went silent after 315V.
Results: 100% went to at least 300V.
Results: 65% (26 of 40) went to the full 450V.
Results: Many showed extreme tension: sweating, trembling, nervous laughter; 3 had seizures.
Conclusion: ordinary people will obey orders from a legitimate authority even when it conflicts with their conscience.
Situational factors (agentic state) explain obedience.
Strength: high control in lab, standardised procedure (prods).
Strength: replicated in variations (e.g. Bridgeport office: 47.5%; experimenter giving orders by phone: 20.5%).
Limitation: ethics - deception, lack of informed consent, psychological harm, right to withdraw made difficult.
Limitation: sample of American men only (gender and culture bias).
Limitation: low ecological validity / artificial task.
Limitation: Orne and Holland argued participants may not have believed the shocks were real (demand characteristics).

intro.text: Milgram (1963) wanted to test how far ordinary people would obey an authority figure instructing them to harm another person.
The sample had 40 American men aged 20 to 50 from New Haven. They were recruited via a newspaper ad and paid $4.50 as a volunteer sample.
Held in a Yale lab. The participant was always the teacher and a confederate named Mr Wallace was the learner. Fake shocks ranged from 15V to 450V in 15V steps.
An experimenter in a grey lab coat used four strict verbal prods like Please continue or You must go on when teachers hesitated.
The learner pounded on the wall at 300V and went silent after 315V. Many participants showed extreme tension, including sweating, trembling, and three full seizures.
100% of participants went to at least 300V, and 65% went all the way to the maximum 450V. Situational factors like an agentic state explain this.

arena.title: Milgram's Study Sorter
arena.instructions: Sort each study detail into Method or Evaluation strengths and limitations.

categoryA.name: Method Detail
categoryA.hint: Part of the original design or procedure

categoryB.name: Evaluation Point
categoryB.hint: A strength or limitation of the study

clues.label: Standardised Prods
clues.claim: The experimenter used the exact same four verbal prods for every participant.
clues.why: High standardisation and control in the lab is a key methodological strength.

clues.label: Bridgeport Variation
clues.claim: The study was replicated in a run-down office, yielding 47.5% obedience.
clues.why: Replications in variations demonstrate reliability and validity of the situational effect.

clues.label: Informed Consent
clues.claim: Participants were fully aware of the true nature of the shock generator.
clues.why: Deception was used and informed consent was lacking, representing an ethical limitation.

clues.label: Sample Bias
clues.claim: The sample consisted entirely of American men aged 20 to 50.
clues.why: Using only American men creates gender and culture bias, lowering population validity.

clues.label: Artificial Task
clues.claim: Giving word-pair tests and fake electric shocks is not a normal everyday activity.
clues.why: This causes low ecological validity because it does not reflect real-life obedience settings.

clues.label: Doubtful Shocks
clues.claim: Orne and Holland argued that participants may not have believed the shocks were real.
clues.why: If participants suspected demand characteristics, it threatens the internal validity of the findings.
